cards.front: What should you know about arousal?
cards.back: A state of physical and psychological readiness and activation. It is the level of excitement, alertness and energy a performer experiences. Arousal exists on a continuum from deep sleep (very low) to extreme excitement or panic (very high).

cards.front: What should you know about inverted-u theory (yerkes-dodson law)?
cards.back: The theory that performance improves as arousal increases, but only up to an optimal point. Beyond this point, further increases in arousal lead to a decline in performance. When graphed, this relationship forms an inverted U shape.

cards.front: What should you know about zone of optimal functioning (zof)?
cards.back: Each individual performer has their own personal zone of optimal arousal where they perform at their best. This zone varies from person to person - some performers need high arousal to perform well, while others perform better at lower arousal levels.

cards.front: What should you know about pe exam tips — arousal and the inverted-u theory?
cards.back: 1. For Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory questions, use subject-specific terminology precisely 2. Support every point with specific evidence or examples 3. Show balanced analysis — consider different perspectives before reaching a conclusion 4. Link your understanding of Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory to real-world contexts where possible 5. For longer answers, plan your response to address all parts of the question
Low (e.g. Needs steady hand, fine control)
Too high or dropping (e.g. Positive self-talk)

Students often say "high arousal always leads to poor performance." Wrong: "If you are too aroused, you will always perform badly." Correct: "For gross and open skills, high arousal is beneficial and optimal. It is only when arousal exceeds the optimal level that performance declines. The optimal level itself varies by skill type."
